title.en: Protocols: Duck Typing You Can Check

description.en: typing.Protocol describes the shape an object must have -- its methods and signatures -- so any class with that shape qualifies without inheriting. Learn what static checkers verify, what runtime isinstance really checks, and when to pick a Protocol over an abstract base class.

story_variants.en:
## Duck Typing, Now With A Safety Net

Python has always said: *if it has a `speak()` method, treat it as a speaker.* That is **duck typing**. It is flexible, but until recently you had no way to *write down* what "speaker" means so that a type checker or a reader could verify it.

`typing.Protocol` (PEP 544) fixes that. A protocol describes the **shape** an object must have -- which methods, with which signatures -- and any class with that shape qualifies. It never has to inherit from the protocol. This is called **structural subtyping**.

### Writing a protocol

```python
from typing import Protocol

class Speaker(Protocol):
    def speak(self) -> str: ...

class Dog:                      # note: no (Speaker) here
    def speak(self) -> str:
        return "Woof"

def greet(s: Speaker) -> str:
    return s.speak()
```

A static checker such as mypy or pyright accepts `greet(Dog())` because `Dog` has a matching `speak`. It rejects `greet(Rock())`. At runtime Python does **not** check annotations, so the protocol on its own changes nothing about how the program runs.

### Checking at runtime: `@runtime_checkable`

If you want `isinstance` to work, add the decorator:

```python
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class Speaker(Protocol):
    def speak(self) -> str: ...

print(isinstance(Dog(), Speaker))   # True
print(isinstance(Rock(), Speaker))  # False
```

**An honest caveat:** `isinstance` against a runtime-checkable protocol only checks that the *names exist*. It does not check argument lists or return types. A class with `speak = 5` passes the check even though calling `speak()` would fail. Use the static checker for the full signature check and `isinstance` for cheap "is this the kind of thing I can call?" tests.

### Protocol vs. abstract base class

| | `abc.ABC` | `Protocol` |
|---|---|---|
| Must the class inherit? | Yes (or be registered) | No |
| Good for | Your own class hierarchy | Describing third-party or duck-typed objects |
| Instantiable? | No, if it has abstract methods | Never |

### Key Takeaways

- A `Protocol` describes a shape; matching classes need no inheritance
- Static type checkers verify the full signature; Python itself ignores annotations
- `@runtime_checkable` enables `isinstance`, but only checks that the method names exist
- You cannot create an instance of a protocol class

under_the_hood.summary: A Protocol describes the methods an object must have. Static checkers verify the whole shape; at runtime isinstance with a runtime-checkable protocol only checks that the names exist.

steps.title: Duck typing, written down
steps.body: Python code has always relied on 'if it has speak(), call it'. A Protocol lets you write that expectation as a type, so tools and readers can check it.

steps.title: Declare the shape
steps.body: The protocol class lists methods with their signatures. Bodies are just `...` because nothing runs; it is a description.

left.label: abc.ABC
left.code:
class Speaker(ABC): ...
class Dog(Speaker): ...  # must inherit

right.label: Protocol
right.code:
class Speaker(Protocol): ...
class Dog: ...  # no inheritance needed

steps.title: The checker compares shapes
steps.body: mypy or pyright looks at Dog, sees speak(self) -> str, and accepts it wherever Speaker is expected. Python itself ignores annotations when the program runs.

steps.title: What isinstance really does
steps.body: With @runtime_checkable, isinstance(obj, Speaker) checks that obj has an attribute called speak. A class with speak = 5 passes, because only the name is checked, not whether it is callable or what it returns.

steps.title: Choose the right tool
steps.body: Use a Protocol to describe objects you do not control or that never share a base class. Use an ABC when you own the hierarchy and want inheritance to enforce the contract.

under_the_hood.takeaway: A Protocol turns duck typing into a checkable contract: any class with the right methods qualifies, no inheritance needed. Remember that isinstance only checks names; the static checker does the full signature check.
